paper_title: Recognition Is Not Grounding: Benchmarking Multilingual Financial Evidence Extraction

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Comparing financial disclosures across languages requires identifying shared accounting concepts and recovering all numerical facts that express them. Existing benchmarks evaluate aspects of these capabilities, but provide limited insight into whether both succeed on the same multilingual evidence. In particular, it remains unclear whether language models can recognize these concepts across languages and exhaustively recover their corresponding numerical evidence from the same contexts. We introduce MULTIFINGROUND, a benchmark designed to investigate this recognition-grounding gap in multilingual financial reports. Constructed from FY2025 disclosures of 90 issuers in English, French, and Greek, MULTIFINGROUND aligns independently authored reports through a shared accounting taxonomy and provides traceable fact-level annotations. The benchmark evaluates financial fact identification, concept recognition, exhaustive fact selection, and concept discrimination without candidate labels. Across 15 evaluated models, eight API and open-weight reference models achieve 97.3-99.4\% concept recognition accuracy, yet miss at least one target fact in 26.6-41.9\% of correctly recognized groups. Further analyses reveal substantial variation in concept discrimination and limited gains from the evaluated finance-specialized models. Our findings demonstrate that strong concept recognition can coexist with incomplete evidence recovery, highlighting the importance of evaluating semantic recognition and evidence completeness together.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Investors and analysts comparing companies across countries need comparable financial information from reports published in different languages (European Securities and Markets Authority, 2026). Multilingual financial information extraction therefore requires models to find 1 numerical facts that express shared accounting concepts across languages and reporting formats. However, these values can appear under different terms, in different table structures, or for different reporting periods (Zhao et al., 2022). Consider French report giving revenue of EUR 280 million for the current year and EUR 250 million for the previous year. model may correctly recognize the revenue concept yet retrieve only the current-year amount, omitting the previous-year value needed to calculate annual growth. The the missing current-year figure is correct, but comparison prevents calculation of annual growth. This illustrates challenge in multilingual numerical grounding: recognizing concept does not guarantee complete recovery of its numerical evidence (Reddy et al., 2024; Choe et al., 2025). Existing benchmarks assess concept linking, extraction, and reasoning  (Table 1)  . These works like FiNER, FNXL, and FinTagging evaluate financial numeral tagging and taxonomy linking (Loukas et al., 2022; Sharma et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2026); FinQA and TAT-QA test numerical reasoning (Chen et al., 2021; Zhu et al., 2021). MultiFin evaluates multilingual financial classification (Jørgensen et al., 2023), while MultiFinBen and XTREME-R include multilingual extraction tasks (Peng et al., 2026; Ruder et al., 2021). However, these works provide limited insight into whether models can recognize shared accounting concepts across languages, recover all corresponding numerical facts, and how performance on these two tasks relates. Examining these questions requires paired evaluation of concept recognition and exhaustive fact selection on the same multilingual contexts. To this end, we introduce MULTIFINGROUND, built from FY2025 European Single Electronic Format (ESEF) reports published by 90 issuers in English, French and Greek. We extract the numerical facts, their contexts and concept annotations, then use shared IFRS concepts to link excerpts across languages and construct paired tasks covering 187 concepts. The excerpts come from different issuers actual disclosures rather than translated versions of the same passage. To assess annotation quality, two financial experts independently review stratified sample, with their agreed corrections and exclusions incorporated into the final dataset (3.8). Models receive the task text and tables without the original iXBRL tags. We design four tasks to distinguish diﬀiculties in numerical interpretation, concept recognition and evidence recovery (Figure 1). Fact Identification (T1) first tests whether models can distinguish financial values from other numbers and identify their accounting attributes. The core paired tasks assess two directions: Concept Recognition (T2a) presents marked numerical facts and asks which accounting concept they share, while Exhaustive Fact Selection (T2b) provides target concept and asks for all corresponding values in the same contexts. This design evaluates each capability separately and examines whether the same model recognizes concept correctly yet omits relevant evidence during extraction. Because T2a provides candidate concepts that may help models identify the answer, Concept Discrimination (T2c) additionally asks which excerpt expresses different concept without providing candidate concept labels. All tasks use independent calls. Diagnostic variants change the evidence languages and taxonomy-label presentation to examine how performance depends on these conditions. Results show that across 15 models, eight models achieve 97.399.4% recognition accuracy yet miss target in 26.641.9% of correctly recognized groups. Further, evidence recovery varies by language. Greek has the lowest recall for seven of these eight models, while concept recognition remains high without English evidence. The evaluated finance-specialized models show limited gains over their corresponding base models under our protocol. These findings highlight the need to evaluate cross-language concept recognition alongside the completeness of numerical evidence recovered in each language. We make three contributions in our work. (1) We construct benchmark linking real multilingual disclosures through shared accounting taxonomy and traceable fact annotations. (2) We pair concept recognition with exhaustive fact selection on matched evidence to measure omissions even when recognizes the correct concept. T1 and T2c complement this pair by testing financial-fact interpretation and distinctions between related concepts 2 without candidate labels, respectively. (3) Evaluating 15 models reveals weaknesses hidden by recognition scores and shows how performance varies with evidence language, label presentation and financial specialization.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Many existing financial benchmarks evaluate how models link numbers to accounting concepts (Loukas et al., 2022; Sharma et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2026), and FinTagging also examines errors across extraction stages. FinQA and TAT-QA test reasoning over financial evidence, with FinQA additionally reporting retrieval recall (Chen et al., 2021; Zhu et al., 2021). MultiFin and MultiFinBen evaluate financial tasks across languages (Jørgensen et al., 2023; Peng et al., 2026). However, these evaluations do not directly show whether models that recognize shared accounting concept can also recover all corresponding numerical facts from the same multilingual evidence  (Table 1)  . Appendix provides fuller comparison.

sections.title: 3.1 Data Collection
sections.content: We collected FY2025 ESEF reports from 30 issuers (reporting companies) per language, each appearing in only one language. All cover full year ending 31 December 2025, with initial factto-concept mappings come from issuer-provided iXBRL tags. Appendix Table 13 lists all 90 issuers, their languages and sectors; Appendix details the English filing index, French CAC 40 and Greek Athens Exchange sources and selection criteria.

sections.title: 3.2 From iXBRL Reports to Evidence
sections.content: We render reports as text and Markdown tables, retaining headers and each facts offsets, concept and accounting attributes. Appendix details extraction, normalization and filtering. ESEF requires individual tags mainly in primary statements; notes use block tags (European Securities and Markets Authority, 2025). Most individually tagged numbers are amounts, per-share amounts or share counts. Initial annotations come from issuer tags and the taxonomy, with expert corrections or exclusions applied to sampled subset (3.8). Issuer-specific extensions, which add concepts not covered by the standard taxonomy, appear only in Fact Identification (T1). The concept-level tasks (T2a, T2b and T2c) use standard ifrs-full concepts. Table 2 summarizes the data. Illustrative example. Consider invented excerpts reporting revenue of EUR 420 million in English, EUR 280 million and 250 million for the current and prior years in French, and EUR 130 million in Greek. Each also contains other figures, such as profit. T1 identifies financial values and their attributes. T2a highlights the revenue figures and asks for their shared concept from candidate labels. T2b provides Revenue and asks for all four values, including the French comparative amount. In separate four-excerpt T2c item, three excerpts mark revenue and one marks profit; the model selects the odd excerpt without candidate concept labels. Appendix gives the full example.

sections.title: Attributes
sections.content: Recovering financial evidence first requires distinguishing financial values from other numbers and interpreting their accounting roles. Therefore, we propose the first task T1, it asks which numbers are financial facts and what accounting roles they have. Each item is passage or table. Every number-like string receives an identifier; splitting and marking rules are in Appendix G. Models identify financial values and return type (monetary, per share, shares), period type (instant: value at date; duration: value over period) and balance (the concepts normal debit or credit side for monetary amounts). For context with numbered instances Nx, the output is f1(x, Nx) = {(n, ban) : bFx}, (1) where bFx Nx contains selected facts and ban is the predicted (type, period, balance) tuple for instance n. These are concept attributes, not properties of the displayed sign. Appendix gives the full definitions and scoring conditions. Block-tagged notes may contain untagged financial values. Untagged numbers are scored as negatives only for clearly excluded categories: years, dates, percentages, references, footnote markers, and counts of years, days or employees.

sections.title: 3.8 Expert Validation
sections.content: Two financial experts independently reviewed stratified 10% sample per task: 131 T1 items, 52 groups shared by T2a/T2b, and 53 T2c items. Sampling covers language, format, data type and item size, with at most one group per concept. Reviewers checked annotations against IFRS definitions, then resolved disagreements through discussion. Appendix details qualifications, sampling, guidelines and uncertainty estimates. Corrections and exclusions apply to the reviewed subset; other items retain automatically derived annotations. All reported benchmark results use this combined final annotation set. Agreement before discussion is κ = 0.87 (T1), 0.74 (T2a), 0.84 (T2b) and 0.88 (T2c). The audit corrects 1.3% of T1 numbers and 2.1% of T2b facts, finds 5.1% of T2a distractors ambiguous, and confirms the odd excerpt for 96.2% of audited T2c items  (Table 12)  . Replacing original with corrected annotations changes reference-model scores by at most 1.4 percentage points on audited subsets. This measures sensitivity to identified errors, not correctness of unreviewed annotations. We evaluate 15 models in four groups (Appendix Table 4). The API models are GPT-5.6 Luna (OpenAI, 2026), Claude Haiku 4.5 (Anthropic, 2025), Gemini 3.8 Flash (Google, 2026) and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (DeepSeek-AI, 2026). Open-weight references are Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026c), Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (Qwen Team, 2026a), Gemma 4 31B IT (Gemma Team et al., 2026) and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B (Qwen Team, 2026b). Finance specialists are Fin-R1 (Liu et al., 2025), Fin-o1-8B (Qian et al., 2025), ODA-FinRL-8B (Cao et al., 2026) and Greek Plutus-8BInstruct (Peng et al., 2025). Their bases are Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Qwen et al., 2024), Qwen38B (Yang et al., 2025) and Llama-Krikri-8BInstruct (Roussis et al., 2025). Each call contains English instructions and original-language evidence, without system prompt, tools, retrieval or history. Prompts request JSON (T1/T2b), letter (T2a) or an excerpt number (T2c); see Appendix B. They average 1.2k input tokens (maximum 3.7k). The output budget is 16,384 tokens including reasoning. We use each models default decoding settings and disable APImodel reasoning. Separate reasoning channels or thinking tags are removed before scoring. The task and scoring protocols are shared, but reasoning and generation settings do not equalize compute (Appendix C). All results use final annotations incorporating expert corrections to audited items. Only the audit sensitivity analysis compares original and corrected annotations.

sections.title: 4.1 Evaluation Metrics
sections.content: For T1, scored numbers belong to seven classes: monetary amounts by period and balance (four), per-share amounts, shares, and none. Omitted numbers receive none; unscored numbers are ignored. We pool per-class scores across items and report seven-class macro-F1. Joint fact F1 requires every attribute to be correct; period and balance accuracy are conditional on correct fact identification. For T2a and T2c, we report accuracy of the chosen option or excerpt. For T2b, we compute precision, recall and F1 against each groups target set. Recall measures the proportion of target facts recovered; precision measures the proportion of selected facts that belong to the target set. The primary score averages group F1 within each concept, then 5 across concepts (concept-macro F1). Complete target coverage requires all target facts to be selected but permits additional incorrect selections. Exactset accuracy requires the predicted set to match the target set exactly, with neither omissions nor extra selections. Per-language precision, recall and F1 pool mentions within each language. Strict protocol. An output is invalid if the request failed, the budget ran out before an answer, the model refused, or the answer does not follow the task format. Invalid outputs are scored as wrong (T1: no predictions; T2a, T2c: incorrect; T2b: F1 and exact match 0). We report invalid rates alongside every score. Uncertainty. T1 intervals resample issuers within language (2,000 bootstrap samples). T2 groups reuse the 30 issuers per language. The graph linking groups to issuers forms single connected component, so we do not report bootstrap intervals for T2. We use exact McNemar tests for paired comparisons of conditions. These item-level pvalues do not account for dependence between items that share issuers. We therefore treat them as exploratory. Baselines. We use two simple baselines. The random baseline samples valid answer uniformly at random. The majority/select-all baseline assigns every number to the most frequent T1 class: monetary amounts with duration period type and credit balance. For T2a and T2c, it always selects the first option or excerpt. For T2b, it selects every numbered fact, ensuring complete target coverage while also including non-target facts.

sections.content: Table 3 reports all 15 models under strict scoring. The eight API/open-weight reference models achieve 97.399.4% T2a accuracy, yet the best T2b scores are 90.4 concept-macro F1 and 71.8% exact-set accuracy. T2c accuracy ranges from 35.695.1%, revealing variation not apparent from recognition accuracy alone (Appendix D.1).

Despite 9799% recognition accuracy, reference models miss target in at least one language in 26.6% (Qwen3.5-122B) to 41.9% (Qwen3.8-27B) of these groups. sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced MULTIFINGROUND to examine whether models can recognize shared accounting concepts and recover all corresponding numerical facts across English, French, and Greek reports. Our results show that models often identify the correct concept while missing relevant values. Evidence recovery also varies by language, with Greek recall lowest for seven of the eight reference models. Models continue to struggle with accounting attributes and distinctions between related concepts, while the evaluated finance-specialized models offer limited improvements. These findings show why multilingual financial extraction should consider not only whether models recognize concepts, but also whether they find all the evidence. sections.title: 5.5 Does Financial Specialization Help?
sections.content: In our evaluation, all four finance-specialized models perform worse than their base models on T1, T2a, and T2c (Figure 6). Fin-R1 improves on T2b by 9.9 macro-F1 points, with larger gains in French and Greek of 12.5 and 14.8 F1 points, respectively. Plutus, despite its Greek specialization, scores 25.4 points below its base model on Greek T1. Its high failure rate partly explains this result: 80% of its T1 outputs are invalid, most of them empty. Overall, we find limited benefits from these finance-specialized models under our evaluation settings for capturing concepts and corresponding numbers.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: This paper has limitations in annotation quality, data coverage, and evaluation. Annotations come from issuer-provided iXBRL tags, which may contain errors or inconsistent concept choices. Financial experts reviewed stratified samples covering 10% of each task, and all reported results incorporate their corrections and exclusions. Errors and ambiguities may remain in the unreviewed portion. Also, T1 leaves untagged amount-like numbers unscored. Most T2 contexts are table windows, and concepts shared across all three languages tend to be common primary-statement concepts. The benchmark covers three languages within one reporting regime. Since language varies together with issuer, sector, and document style, differences between single-language conditions cannot be attributed to language alone.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: The benchmark uses public regulatory filings and the IFRS Accounting Taxonomy. We document the access conditions for each source. Where full documents cannot be redistributed, the release provides annotations, source information and instructions for reconstructing the inputs. Reports contain company information only; no personal data are part of the benchmark inputs. The two financial experts who reviewed the annotations are co-authors of this paper. Benchmark scores do not establish suitability for financial reporting compliance and do not replace professional review.

sections.title: Use of AI Assistants
sections.content: The authors used AI assistants, including ChatGPT, to support language polishing, brainstorming, and LaTeX editing. All technical claims, experimental results, analysis, and final writing decisions were reviewed and verified by the authors.

The expert first checks whether every highlighted number reports the target concept. If not, the item is flagged and handled as in T2b. The expert then rates each of the three distractors against all groups of that concept. The ratings are too easy (ruled out without reading the excerpts: different statement or nature, data type or direction, or an industry item that fits none of the issuers), good (plausible at first sight, ruled out by the excerpts or definitions), hard but fair (a sibling, current versus non-current, or narrower or broader neighbour that is clearly wrong for every group), and ambiguous (could also be correct for at least one group). Distractors rated too easy or ambiguous are replaced by plausible but clearly wrong concept of the same data type, usually from the same statement. Option sets that give away the answer count as too easy. One example is general concept presented alongside three industry-specific concepts. Test question: Would accept this option if model chose it? If yes or maybe, the distractor is ambiguous. T2b (labels of all facts). For every numbered fact the expert answers: Is tagging this number with the target concept correct under IFRS? Labels: is the concept; not (a different line item, total that includes the concept, component of it, movement instead of balance or vice versa, different period type); ambiguous. number that equals target in value but sits in another row is judged by its row label. When the issuer used more specific concept that fits better, the expert labels that number not. Each context receives verdict: usable, needs fix or drop. Reasons to drop context include an incomplete table, missing headers or far too many numbers. group is removed if any of its contexts is dropped. The expert also rates the diﬀiculty of the group (too easy, adequate, too hard or too large). T2c (odd excerpt). The expert answers: Do the marked numbers of exactly three excerpts report the same concept, and those of the remaining excerpt different one? Labels: valid (the three excerpts report and the odd excerpt reports d, which is clearly different under the definitions); ambiguous (d could also be reported as in that context, or one of the three excerpts could report d); invalid (another excerpt is the odd one, or the marked numbers of an excerpt do not report its concept). sections.title: H Extended Related Work
sections.content: Financial extraction and reasoning. FiNER and FNXL assign XBRL concepts to numbers in text. Instruction tuning with information about each concept extends this tagging approach to large label sets (Loukas et al., 2022; Sharma et al., 2023; Khatuya et al., 2024). FinTagging separates extraction and typing from taxonomy linking across text and tables, and examines error propagation through this pipeline (Wang et al., 2026). These resources test semantic precision and extraction recall within one language. Our paired evaluation examines the relationship between concept recognition and exhaustive numerical evidence recovery on matched multilingual contexts. We also test whether models distinguish related concepts without candidate labels. FinQA and TAT-QA test financial evidence use and arithmetic (Chen et al., 2021; Zhu et al., 2021); FinQA also reports supporting-fact retrieval recall. We instead examine target coverage conditional on correct concept recognition, without requiring arithmetic. Multilingual evaluation. XLM-R, XTREME-R, and multilingual E5 address multilingual representations, transfer, and retrieval (Conneau et al., 2020; Ruder et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2024). MultiFin uses shared set of financial topics across languages. MultiFinBen covers multilingual financial understanding, extraction and reasoning (Jørgensen et al., 2023; Peng et al., 2026). We focus on individual numbers and the accounting concepts they express. We match excerpts from different issuers by concept, without requiring parallel text. This lets us relate concept recognition to target coverage on the same evidence and assess concept discrimination separately. Because these contexts come from different issuers, differences in coverage may also reflect sector and document diﬀiculty, rather than language alone. package, and foreign-registered constituents filing in English. Greek reports are consolidated filings from Athens Exchange issuers across eleven sectors, generally smaller companies than those in the other collections. We verified that every report covered full year (a 365-day context ending on 31 December 2025) and assigned sectors manually. Evidence extraction. We render each inline XBRL report in browser running without graphical interface. HTML tables are converted to Markdown with their headers. On pages converted from PDF, we group text by position to recover lines. We then reconstruct paragraphs or tables by grouping numbers whose right edges align. Running text is split at sentence boundaries beyond 1,500 characters. Columns containing numbers but no tagged facts are dropped to exclude untagged parent-company figures alongside consolidated data. Normalization covers Unicode NFC, non-breaking and thin spaces, zero-width and control characters, soft hyphens, private-use characters, ligatures and the Unicode minus sign. Each tagged fact retains its visible-text offsets, concept, datatype, period type and balance. Attributes come from the IFRS Accounting Taxonomy 2024 or the issuer schema for extensions. Empty nil facts without visible text are excluded. T1 marking. Tables exceeding 60 tagged facts are split by row with headers repeated. Every numberlike string receives an identifier ([N1] 1,234); dash-only nil displays are not marked. displayed number counts once even if it has multiple tags. T2a contexts and sampling. context is passage or table window containing at most five header rows and the three rows above and below the first target row. Contexts with another concept tagged on target number are excluded. Groups are sampled with fixed seed and without reusing an issuer for that concept within language. T2a distractors. Distractors share the targets datatype and an IFRS presentation section and have the closest English labels. We exclude calculation relatives within two steps, concepts tagged interchangeably on the same row label, and options with indistinguishable labels in any language. Options are fixed per concept, with balanced order. T2c distractors. The distractor shares parent in the calculation hierarchy or has similar label. It must be neither an ancestor nor descendant of the target, and issuers must not use the two interchangeably. Their labels must also differ in each
